title: Your first Spring Boot project
intro: Spring Boot gives you a practical way to build Java web applications without wiring every framework component by hand. In this lesson, you will create your first Spring Boot project, expose a REST endpoint, configure it, and run it from IntelliJ IDEA Community or the terminal.
body:
## What Spring Boot adds to Spring

Spring is a large Java framework for building applications. It provides concepts such as dependency injection, application configuration, web handling, validation and many other building blocks.

**Spring Boot is a layer on top of Spring that makes starting and configuring a Spring application much easier.** Instead of manually configuring many parts of the application, Spring Boot uses sensible defaults and automatic configuration.

Three Spring Boot ideas are especially important at the beginning:

- **Auto-configuration** detects the dependencies in your project and configures common components automatically.
- **Starters** are dependency bundles for common application types. For example, Spring Web gives you the dependencies needed to build web applications and REST APIs.
- **Embedded Tomcat** lets your application run its own web server. You do not need to install a separate Tomcat server just to start a Spring Boot application.

This is one reason Spring Boot feels different from older Java web application setups. You can run the application as a normal Java process and immediately have an HTTP server available.

## Generate the project

The easiest way to create a standard Spring Boot project is [start.spring.io](https://start.spring.io/), the Spring Initializr service.

Create a project with these settings:

- Project: Maven
- Language: Java
- Spring Boot: the current Spring Boot 3 release available in the generator
- Group: for example `hu.softwaredevelopment`
- Artifact: `task-manager`
- Packaging: Jar
- Java: 21

Add these dependencies:

- Spring Web
- Validation
- Spring Boot DevTools
- Spring Boot Actuator

The generator creates a complete Maven project that you can download and open in IntelliJ IDEA Community.

The exact Spring Boot patch version can change over time. For this course, the important requirement is **Spring Boot 3 running on Java 21**.

The official Spring Boot documentation is available at [docs.spring.io](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/).

## Open the project in IntelliJ IDEA Community

Extract the downloaded project and open its directory in IntelliJ IDEA Community.

IntelliJ will recognise the Maven project from `pom.xml`. Maven is the build tool that manages the project's dependencies, compilation, tests and packaging.

You do not need IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate for the workflow used in this course. Community Edition can run the Java application and can use the Maven wrapper included in the generated project.

The generated project normally contains a Maven wrapper. On macOS or Linux you can run it with:

~~~shell
./mvnw spring-boot:run
~~~

On Windows, the corresponding command is:

~~~shell
mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run
~~~

You can also run the application's main class directly from IntelliJ.

## Understand the project structure

A new Spring Boot project has a structure similar to this:

~~~diagram
{"type": "tree", "title": "A fresh Spring Boot project", "root": {"label": "task-api/", "children": [{"label": "pom.xml", "sub": "dependencies"}, {"label": "mvnw", "sub": "Maven wrapper"}, {"label": "src/main/", "highlight": true, "children": [{"label": "java/…", "sub": "TaskApiApplication.java"}, {"label": "resources/", "sub": "application.properties"}]}, {"label": "src/test/", "children": [{"label": "java/…", "sub": "tests"}]}]}}
~~~

~~~text
task-manager/
├── pom.xml
├── mvnw
├── mvnw.cmd
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/
    │   │   └── hu/softwaredevelopment/taskmanager/
    │   │       └── TaskManagerApplication.java
    │   └── resources/
    │       └── application.properties
    └── test/
        └── java/
~~~

`src/main/java` contains the production Java source code.

`src/main/resources` contains application resources such as configuration files.

`application.properties` is the default configuration file. You can also use `application.yml`, which represents configuration in YAML format.

`src/test/java` contains automated tests.

The `pom.xml` file describes the Maven project and its dependencies.

## The main application class

The generated application contains a class similar to this:

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "What happens when you press Run", "steps": [{"label": "main()", "sub": "SpringApplication.run(…)"}, {"label": "Component scan", "sub": "finds @RestController, @Service …"}, {"label": "Auto-configuration", "sub": "web server, JSON, DB from the classpath"}, {"label": "Tomcat starts", "sub": "listening on :8080"}]}
~~~

~~~java
package hu.softwaredevelopment.taskmanager;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class TaskManagerApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(TaskManagerApplication.class, args);
    }
}
~~~

The `main` method is still the normal Java entry point. The important difference is what happens inside it.

`SpringApplication.run(...)` starts the Spring application. Spring creates its application context, applies configuration, discovers components and starts the embedded web server.

`@SpringBootApplication` is a convenient annotation that combines several important Spring annotations, including configuration and component scanning and Spring Boot's auto-configuration.

You can think of it as telling Spring Boot: **this is the main application and you should build the application context around it.**

## Your first REST controller

A **REST API** is an HTTP API where clients interact with resources and operations using HTTP requests. We will build the task manager as a REST API.

A controller is a class responsible for handling HTTP requests.

Create a class called `HelloController`:

~~~java
package hu.softwaredevelopment.taskmanager;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class HelloController {

    @GetMapping("/api/hello")
    public HelloResponse hello() {
        return new HelloResponse("Hello from Spring Boot!");
    }

    public record HelloResponse(String message) {}
}
~~~

`@RestController` tells Spring that this class handles web requests and that its return values should be written to the HTTP response body.

`@GetMapping("/api/hello")` maps HTTP GET requests for `/api/hello` to the `hello()` method.

The method returns a Java record. Spring Boot's web support automatically serialises the record into JSON.

The response will look approximately like this:

~~~json
{
  "message": "Hello from Spring Boot!"
}
~~~

This is an important moment: **a Java method has become an HTTP endpoint without you writing a servlet or manually converting the object to JSON.** Spring Boot is doing that work for you.

## Run the application

Start the application from IntelliJ by running the main application class.

~~~callout ide Run and stop from IntelliJ
Click the green ▶ next to `TaskApiApplication`. The **Run** tool window shows the log — look for `Tomcat started on port 8080`. **Ctrl/⌘+F2** stops the app; if the port is still busy, another instance is running.
~~~

Alternatively, use the Maven wrapper:

~~~shell
./mvnw spring-boot:run
~~~

You should see startup messages in the terminal. Among them, Spring Boot will report that Tomcat has started and that the application is listening on port `8080` by default.

Open this address in your browser:

~~~text
http://localhost:8080/api/hello
~~~

Because the endpoint uses GET, the browser can call it directly.

You can also test it from the terminal:

~~~shell
curl http://localhost:8080/api/hello
~~~

You should receive JSON similar to:

~~~json
{"message":"Hello from Spring Boot!"}
~~~

`curl` is a command-line HTTP client. It is useful because it lets you test an API without needing a frontend.

## Configuration with application.properties

Spring Boot applications are heavily configuration-driven. The simplest configuration format is `application.properties`.

For example:

~~~properties
spring.application.name=task-manager
server.port=8080
~~~

Each line contains a property name, an equals sign, and a value.

The `server.port` property controls the HTTP server port. If you change it to `8081`, your application will be available at:

~~~text
http://localhost:8081/api/hello
~~~

You can also use `application.yml` instead of `application.properties`:

~~~yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: task-manager
server:
  port: 8080
~~~

You normally choose one configuration style for a particular project. Both are supported by Spring Boot.

## Profiles

Different environments often need different configuration. Your local development environment might use one database, while production uses another.

Spring profiles allow you to activate environment-specific configuration.

The default file can contain common settings:

~~~properties
spring.application.name=task-manager
~~~

You can create:

~~~text
application-dev.properties
~~~

and put development-specific settings there:

~~~properties
server.port=8081
~~~

Then activate the `dev` profile with:

~~~properties
spring.profiles.active=dev
~~~

Or pass it when starting the application:

~~~shell
./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev
~~~

A profile is simply a named set of configuration values that can be activated for a particular environment or use case.

Later, we will use profiles for configuration such as local database settings versus production settings.

## Environment variables

You should not put secrets such as production database passwords directly into source-controlled configuration files.

Spring Boot can read configuration from environment variables. Environment variables are values provided by the operating system or deployment environment.

For example, a configuration property can be represented by an environment variable using Spring Boot's relaxed binding rules:

~~~properties
server.port=8080
~~~

can be overridden by:

~~~shell
SERVER_PORT=8081 ./mvnw spring-boot:run
~~~

The environment variable has higher priority than the value in `application.properties`.

This is useful when deploying the same application to different environments. The application code stays the same while the environment supplies the appropriate configuration.

## Actuator and the health endpoint

We added Spring Boot Actuator as a dependency when generating the project.

**Actuator provides operational endpoints that help you inspect and monitor a running Spring Boot application.** One of the most useful endpoints is the health endpoint.

By default, you can access:

~~~text
http://localhost:8080/actuator/health
~~~

A healthy application normally returns JSON similar to:

~~~json
{
  "status": "UP"
}
~~~

This endpoint becomes particularly useful when your application is deployed to a server. A monitoring system or deployment platform can check whether the application is responding.

Actuator has many other capabilities, but we will keep the initial setup simple. As the application becomes more complex, operational information becomes increasingly useful.

## Why DevTools is included

Spring Boot DevTools provides development-time conveniences. One common feature is automatic application restart when classpath files change.

This can make the development feedback loop faster: change code, compile it, and let the development application restart rather than manually stopping and starting it every time.

DevTools is intended for development. It should not be treated as a production feature or a replacement for a proper deployment process.

## Common startup errors

### Port 8080 is already in use

A common first error looks similar to:

~~~text
Web server failed to start. Port 8080 was already in use.
~~~

This means another process is already listening on that port.

You can either stop the other application or configure another port:

~~~properties
server.port=8081
~~~

Then access the application on port 8081 instead.

### A dependency is missing

If you use `@RestController` but Spring cannot find the required web classes, check `pom.xml` and make sure the Spring Web dependency was added.

The Spring Initializr normally handles this correctly, which is one reason it is preferable to manually assembling a new Spring Boot project's dependencies.

After changing Maven dependencies, let IntelliJ reload the Maven project. You can also run the Maven wrapper from the terminal to verify that the project builds.

### The application starts but the endpoint returns 404

A `404 Not Found` means Spring did not find a matching endpoint.

Check the URL carefully:

~~~text
/api/hello
~~~

Also check that the controller is inside the package scanned by the application. If your main class is in `hu.softwaredevelopment.taskmanager`, placing the controller in a child package such as `hu.softwaredevelopment.taskmanager.web` is a straightforward convention.

## Common mistakes

### Putting controllers outside the scanned package

Spring Boot's component scanning starts from the package of the main application class. Keep your application classes under the main package unless you have a specific reason to configure scanning differently.

### Hard-coding production secrets

Never commit passwords, API keys or other sensitive values into Git just because the application works locally. Use environment variables or another appropriate secret-management mechanism for deployment.

### Confusing the browser with the backend

When you visit `/api/hello` in a browser, the browser is the client. The Java application is the server. The browser is not executing your controller code; it is sending an HTTP request and displaying the response.

### Thinking Spring Boot requires a separate Tomcat installation

For a normal Spring Boot web application, embedded Tomcat is included through the web stack. Starting the Java application starts the web server too.

### Changing configuration but using the wrong profile

If a value in `application-dev.properties` does not appear to work, check whether the `dev` profile is actually active. A profile-specific file is not automatically active merely because the file exists.

## What you have built

At this point, you have a working Java web application with an HTTP server, configuration, a REST endpoint and a health endpoint.

The architecture is intentionally small. We have not introduced services, repositories or a database yet. That is deliberate: before adding layers, you should understand what the basic Spring Boot application is doing.

In the next lesson, we will build more useful REST controllers for the task manager. You will learn how HTTP methods, path variables, query parameters and request bodies map to Java methods and objects.

The important mental model is simple:

~~~text
HTTP request
    ↓
Spring Boot
    ↓
@RestController method
    ↓
Java object
    ↓
JSON HTTP response
~~~

Once this flow is comfortable, the rest of the backend course becomes much easier to understand.
takeaways: Spring Boot simplifies Spring applications through auto-configuration, starters and an embedded web server.
Spring Initializr can generate a Maven project with Java 21 and the dependencies needed for a REST application.
A @RestController maps HTTP requests to Java methods and can return objects that Spring serialises as JSON.
application.properties or application.yml controls configuration, while profiles and environment variables support different environments.
Spring Boot Actuator provides operational endpoints such as /actuator/health for checking application health.

quiz.question: What is one of the main things Spring Boot's auto-configuration does?
options: It automatically writes Java source code for your controllers
It detects the application's dependencies and configures common components using sensible defaults
It replaces Java with JavaScript in the backend
It creates a PostgreSQL database automatically
quiz.explanation: Auto-configuration examines the application and its dependencies and configures common Spring components automatically.

quiz.question: What does @RestController tell Spring?
options: The class should handle HTTP requests and return response data
The class should only be used for database migrations
The class must contain the main method
The class should be compiled as TypeScript
quiz.explanation: @RestController marks a class as a web controller whose methods can handle HTTP requests and whose return values are written to responses.

options: POST requests to /api/hello
Any request to port 8080 regardless of its path
GET requests to /api/hello
Only requests from IntelliJ IDEA
quiz.explanation: @GetMapping maps HTTP GET requests to the specified path to the annotated method.

quiz.question: Which URL is the default Spring Boot Actuator health endpoint?
options: /health
/api/health
/actuator/status
/actuator/health
quiz.explanation: With Actuator enabled, the health endpoint is available at /actuator/health by default.

quiz.question: What happens when SERVER_PORT=8081 is supplied as an environment variable while application.properties contains server.port=8080?
options: The application always uses 8080 because properties files have highest priority
The application uses 8081 because the environment variable can override the properties value
The application refuses to start because two ports are configured
The application starts on both ports
quiz.explanation: Spring Boot's externalised configuration gives environment variables higher priority than values from application.properties in this situation.

exercise.title: Build a properties resolver
exercise.task: Write two TypeScript functions that mirror a small but important part of Spring Boot configuration. First, implement parseProperties(text), which turns application.properties-style text into a plain object. Each non-ignored line contains one key=value pair. Trim the key and value. Ignore blank lines and lines whose first non-whitespace character is # or !. A value may contain = characters, so only the first = separates the key from the value. If a key appears more than once, the later value wins. Second, implement resolveProperty(key, sources), where sources is an array of property objects ordered from lowest to highest priority, for example [defaults, profile, environment]. Return the value from the highest-priority source that defines the key, and return undefined when no source defines it. This TypeScript exercise mirrors how you reason about configuration in Spring Boot; the actual Spring Boot configuration is handled by the framework in the Java project.
exercise.hint: For parseProperties(), split the input into lines and trim each line before checking whether it should be ignored. Find the first = with indexOf() so later = characters remain part of the value. For duplicate keys, simply assigning result[key] again makes the later value win. For resolveProperty(), search the sources backwards because the last source has the highest priority.

tests.name: It ignores blank and comment lines
It keeps equals signs inside values
It lets later duplicate keys win
It resolves the highest priority source
